steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation turns one OH into OH₂⁺, which can leave as water. The two OH groups of pinacol are the same, so either can be protonated.
Water leaves and a tertiary carbocation forms. In an unsymmetrical diol, the OH that leaves is the one giving the more stable cation.
Also correct: the methyl group can move as water leaves, in one step. The textbook picture has the tertiary cation first.

A methyl group moves with its bonding pair to the cation next door. The cation it leaves behind is stabilised by the oxygen lone pair: it is a protonated ketone, much more stable than any carbocation. This is what drives the rearrangement.
Loss of the proton gives pinacolone and returns the sulfuric acid.

title: Pinacol rearrangement
subtitle: A 1,2-diol in acid: a methyl group moves and a ketone forms
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36

reactants.caption: pinacol (2,3-dimethylbutane-2,3-diol) + sulfuric acid
hintTiers: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group, but water is a good one. What does the acid do to an OH group?
One OH oxygen uses a lone pair to take the proton from sulfuric acid, and that O–H pair stays on the acid's oxygen. Two arrows.
Lone pair of the OH oxygen without the drawn hydrogen → new bond to the acidic proton of H₂SO₄; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the sulfuric acid oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Turn one OH group into a leaving group.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydroxide is a poor leaving group: an OH does not leave on its own. Protonate it first so that it leaves as water.

oxonium-ion.caption: protonated pinacol + hydrogensulfate
hintTiers: The protonated OH can now leave as a neutral water molecule. What kind of carbon is left behind?
The C–O bond breaks and its pair goes to the oxygen. One arrow: a tertiary carbocation.
C–O bond to the protonated oxygen → a lone pair on that oxygen, leaving a tertiary cation.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton off the other OH group does not lead anywhere yet. Let water leave first.
An SN2 reaction at a crowded tertiary carbon is not possible. Water leaves on its own to give a carbocation.

tertiary-cation.caption: tertiary carbocation + water + hydrogensulfate
hintTiers: The neighbouring carbon carries an OH group. If a methyl group moves across with its bonding pair, which atom can then stabilise the new cation?
A methyl group on the carbinol carbon moves to the cation (a 1,2-shift), and the OH lone pair makes a C=O π bond. Two arrows.
C–CH₃ bond of the carbinol carbon → new bond from that methyl to the cationic carbon; OH oxygen lone pair → C=O π bond.
tertiary-cation.learnerPrompt: The key step: a group moves onto the cation.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water adding back just reverses the last step. Look at the groups on the neighbouring carbon.
The OH group stays where it is: it is the group that will stabilise the new cation, by becoming C=O. A methyl group migrates.
Hydrogensulfate is a weak nucleophile, and the cation finds a much better way to become stable: the 1,2-shift gives a cation stabilised by the oxygen lone pair.

protonated-ketone.caption: protonated pinacolone + water + hydrogensulfate
hintTiers: The positive oxygen still carries a proton. Which base was released in the first step?
The hydrogensulfate oxygen takes the proton; the O–H pair stays on the carbonyl oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydrogensulfate oxygen lone pair → new bond to the drawn H; O–H bond → a lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water can take this proton as well. Here hydrogensulfate, made in the first step, takes it back, so the acid is regenerated: it is a catalyst.

mechanismSummary: One OH group of pinacol is protonated and leaves as water, giving a tertiary carbocation. A methyl group on the neighbouring carbon moves across with its bonding pair (a 1,2-shift), leaving a cation next to the remaining OH. The oxygen lone pair stabilises it as a protonated ketone, and loss of the proton gives pinacolone. The C=O bond formed is the driving force.
